essentials: The SFDR is a **disclosure regulation** for the financial sector: asset managers, insurers, pension providers and advisers must explain how they deal with sustainability risks and impacts.
It works at two levels: the **firm** (policies and adverse impacts) and the **product** (each fund or mandate).

Products are known by the article they disclose under: **Article 6** (no sustainability claim), **Article 8** (promotes environmental or social characteristics), **Article 9** (sustainable investment as objective).
These articles were never meant as labels, but the market uses them as such. That misuse is the main reason for the **SFDR 2.0** reform.

sections.title: Why it exists
text: The EU wants private capital to finance the transition. For that, investors must be able to tell which products take sustainability seriously. The SFDR, in application since March 2021, obliges providers to publish standardised information so that claims can be checked and compared.
It regulates what must be **said**, not how money must be **invested**. A fund may invest in anything; it just has to describe its approach truthfully in a prescribed format.

sections.title: Who is covered
points: **Financial market participants**: managers of investment funds (UCITS and alternative funds), portfolio managers, insurers offering investment products, pension providers.
**Financial advisers**: firms that advise on investments or insurance-based investment products.
Non-EU managers are caught when they market funds in the EU.

sections.title: Firm-level disclosures
points: **Sustainability risk policy** (Article 3): how the firm integrates sustainability risks into investment decisions or advice.

**Principal adverse impacts** (Article 4): whether the firm considers the negative effects of its investments on the environment and society. Firms with more than 500 employees must publish an annual statement with defined indicators; smaller firms may explain why they do not.
**Remuneration** (Article 5): how pay policies are consistent with the integration of sustainability risks.

What it claims

after: The information appears in three places: **pre-contractual documents** such as the prospectus, the **website**, and **periodic reports**. The Level 2 rules that have applied since January 2023 prescribe templates for Article 8 and 9 products.

sections.title: The three building blocks behind the wording
points: **Sustainable investment** (Article 2(17)): an investment in an activity that contributes to an environmental or social objective, does not significantly harm any such objective, in a company with good governance. The definition leaves much to the manager's own methodology.

**Principal adverse impact indicators**: a set of mandatory indicators, such as greenhouse gas emissions, fossil fuel exposure, board gender diversity and violations of international norms, plus optional ones.
**Taxonomy alignment**: Article 8 and 9 products with environmental aims disclose what share of their investments is Taxonomy-aligned. Zero is a permitted answer.

sections.title: Where it went wrong
text: Article 8 is very broad. A fund that excludes a few sectors and a fund with a demanding strategy can both be Article 8. Because distributors and investors treated the articles as quality labels, large parts of the market were classified as Article 8, and the ‘sustainable investment’ definition was applied differently by every manager. In 2022 and 2023 many funds were moved from Article 9 to Article 8 after regulators clarified their expectations.

As a stop-gap, **ESMA's guidelines on fund names** require funds that use ESG or sustainability terms in their name to invest at least 80% in line with those terms and to apply defined exclusions. The structural answer is the SFDR revision.

terms.text: The product providers covered by the SFDR, such as fund managers and insurers.
An environmental, social or governance event that could reduce the value of an investment. The outside-in view.
The negative effect of investment decisions on sustainability factors. The inside-out view.
Promotes environmental or social characteristics. Often called ‘light green’, a term the regulation does not use.
Has sustainable investment as its objective. Often called ‘dark green’.
Delegated Regulation (EU) 2022/1288, with the detailed templates and indicators.
Sound management structures, employee relations, staff remuneration and tax compliance at investee companies.

mistakes.wrong: Article 8 and Article 9 are sustainability labels.
mistakes.right: They are disclosure categories. The regulation sets no minimum quality for either.

mistakes.wrong: An Article 9 fund invests only in Taxonomy-aligned activities.
mistakes.right: It invests in ‘sustainable investments’ as defined by the SFDR, which is wider and partly defined by the manager. Its Taxonomy-aligned share can be low.

mistakes.wrong: The SFDR tells managers what they may invest in.
mistakes.right: It only requires transparency about the approach taken.

mistakes.wrong: Sustainability risk and adverse impact are the same thing.
mistakes.right: Risk is the effect of sustainability matters on the investment. Adverse impact is the effect of the investment on the world.

practice: **Classify every product** and keep the reasoning on file. Supervisors ask why a product is Article 8 rather than 6 or 9.
Make sure the **three disclosures are consistent**: prospectus annex, website and periodic report must tell the same story.
Define and document your **sustainable investment methodology**: contribution, do no significant harm, good governance.
Check **fund names** against ESMA's guidelines before launch.
Map **data sources** for each adverse impact indicator and mark where estimates are used.
Follow the **SFDR 2.0** negotiations and test where each product would land under the new categories.

quiz.q: What kind of regulation is the SFDR?
options: A labelling scheme for green funds
A disclosure regulation for financial market participants and advisers
A capital requirement for banks
A ban on investments in fossil fuels
quiz.why: It requires transparency at firm and product level. It neither labels products nor restricts investments.

options: It promotes environmental or social characteristics
It has sustainable investment as its objective
It makes no sustainability claim
It invests only in government bonds
quiz.why: Article 9 covers products whose objective is sustainable investment. Promoting characteristics is Article 8.

options: Losses a fund suffers from climate events
Negative effects of investment decisions on the environment and society
Fees charged for sustainable products
The main risks listed in a prospectus
quiz.why: They describe the inside-out view: what the investments do to sustainability factors.

quiz.q: Which firms must publish a principal adverse impact statement, without the option to explain instead?
options: All firms
Firms with more than 500 employees
Firms managing Article 9 products
Firms listed on a stock exchange
quiz.why: Above 500 employees the statement is mandatory. Smaller firms may explain why they do not consider adverse impacts.

quiz.q: Why is it misleading to call Article 8 a label?
options: Because the article sets no minimum standard; very different strategies fit under it
Because Article 8 products are not allowed to mention sustainability
Because only ESMA may award labels
Because Article 8 applies only to insurers
quiz.why: Article 8 is a disclosure trigger. A light exclusion policy and a demanding strategy can both fall under it.

quiz.q: Where must product-level information be disclosed?
options: Only in the annual report
In pre-contractual documents, on the website and in periodic reports
Only on request
In a filing to the European Central Bank
quiz.why: The SFDR prescribes all three, and they have to be consistent with one another.

quiz.q: Can an Article 8 fund report a Taxonomy-aligned share of 0%?
options: No, at least 10% is required
No, Article 8 funds must be fully aligned
Yes, it must disclose the share, whatever it is
Yes, but only in the first year
quiz.why: The duty is to disclose the share, not to reach a minimum.
